title: fix(safe-queue): map a null `to` from the Queue Service to the zero address
description:
## Summary

The Queue Service returns `to: null` for transactions with no recipient, while the Transaction Service returns the zero address for the same case. The queue entity schema rejected `null`, so response validation broke whenever the Queue Service returned such a transaction.

`to` in `SafeQueueMultisigTransactionSchema` now accepts `null` or a missing value and transforms it to viem's `zeroAddress`, keeping the domain `MultisigTransaction.to` non-nullable and the client-facing shape identical across both upstreams. A nullable `to` was avoided because it would require changing the shared `TransactionBaseSchema`, every mapper, and the client contract; mapping to the zero address instead matches what the Transaction Service already does.

## Changes

- `src/modules/safe-queue/entities/multisig-transaction.entity.ts`: `to` now accepts `null`/missing and transforms to `zeroAddress`.
- `src/modules/safe-queue/entities/__tests__/multisig-transaction.entity.spec.ts`: new spec covering null, missing, checksummed and invalid `to` values.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

findings.claim: A batch-path test case (a chunk containing a null-to row should be kept rather than dropped) and a single-tx case (a pending tx served from the queue should resolve to = zeroAddress) should be added to cover the regression.

There is no documentation in the repository confirming what a null to field means upstream in the Queue Service (i.e., whether it sends to: null, omits the key entirely, or something else), which makes it unclear whether mapping null to the zero address is the correct interpretation.

Before this fix, a transaction with to: null caused the batch chunk's safeParse to fail, dropping the whole chunk; in resolveMultisigTransaction (src/modules/safe/domain/safe.repository.ts:603) this forced a fallback to the Transaction Service. The new spec only verifies the schema in isolation, and neither safe-queue.service.spec.ts nor safe.repository.spec.ts pins down the batch-drop or fallback behavior, so the actual regression the user observed has no test coverage.

The schema silently maps an upstream `null` `to` value to the zero address without any comment explaining why, and the commit message has no body either, even though every other nullable address field in this schema uses `NullableAddressSchema` instead, making this deliberate difference unexplained; a one-line comment noting that the Queue Service returns null where the Transaction Service returns the zero address would clarify the intent.

If the Queue Service does not omit the to key (only sends it as null), .nullable() should be used instead of .nullish(), and the test covering a missing to key should be dropped since it would no longer reflect valid input.

The PR body should include a line clarifying what a null to value means upstream (in the Queue Service), since this assumption underlies the whole fix and is not otherwise verifiable from the codebase.

The test casts a value with `as `0x${string}`` while no other spec in the repo uses that form, whereas `toLowerCase() as Address` appears 52 times elsewhere, so the cast style is inconsistent with existing convention; using `import type { Address } from 'viem'` and `as Address` would match it.

Using .nullish() instead of .nullable() means the schema accepts a body with no to key at all, not just an explicit to: null. Previously such a body failed to parse and fell back to the Transaction Service, but now it parses successfully and a pending transaction is served from the queue with its recipient mapped to the zero address (src/modules/safe-queue/mappers/transaction.mapper.ts:40), which could misrepresent the transaction's recipient if the Queue Service does not actually omit the field for this reason.

It is unclear whether the zero address is actually the correct semantic meaning of a null `to` value, since the mapper passes `tx.to` straight through to clients, so if null could mean something other than 'sent to the zero address' this mapping would hide that distinction from callers; this should be confirmed against the Queue Service contract and stated in the explanatory comment.
